answer:
1. The image shows a grid of tiles, one for each month from January 1991 to July 2016. Each tile is lit if buying a home that month left the buyer ahead of a renter after ten years. It is dark if the renter came out ahead. The caption says it uses FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. It is labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. The grid itself barely changes across the six frames. The layout, the lit and dark regions and the dates stay the same. The only visible changes are a few tiles in one column that brighten and dim slightly. A caption appears in frame 4 and stays through frame 6: "2002 to 2007: 6 of 72 (8.3%)". That is a highlighted stretch of months, marked by a column of orange tiles, in which the buyer was ahead after ten years in only 6 of 72 months.

3. The meaning is that whether buying beat renting depended heavily on when you bought. For most of the lit stretch on the left, buyers were ahead after ten years. For purchases around 2002–2007, the buyer was ahead in only about 8% of months. That period was the run-up to the housing bust. The dark tiles on the right are the months with no ten-year result, because the data ends in July 2016. Some of those tiles may mean the renter was ahead, though I can't tell from the image. The image doesn't show what the tile colors would look like for a purchase in 2026.

4. A viewer might take away that the timing and price level of a purchase matter a lot, and that buying isn't automatically cheaper than renting. The image gives no recommendation to buy or to rent, and it gives no numbers for your case, such as interest, property tax, insurance or repairs.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the history and the 6-of-72 statistic. Its on-screen text says "history, not a forecast", which discourages reading it as advice.
